definition: Apprehend means to seize or arrest someone.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word apprehend. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know apprehend should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Two off-duty constables apprehended the pickpocket in the theater lobby before the intermission crowd noticed a single missing watch.
To detain someone is to hold them briefly — an hour in a side room while papers are checked; detain stops short of apprehend, which is the formal seizure of a suspect.
Incarcerate goes further than apprehend: an arrest begins custody, while incarceration is the long lock-and-key that a court may order afterward.

Arrest is the plain legal word for taking someone into custody once charges attach — it is what the law does and what officers say. Apprehend does the same work in a more formal register: the word of reports and dispatches, and its object is always a suspect.

Collar is the informal, almost gleeful word — an officer collars a thief in the act, hand on the scruff of his coat. Apprehend is its opposite in register: the same seizure of a suspect, but written up formally for the report, the dispatch, and the courtroom.

The warrant sat unserved for a year until a hotel clerk recognized the forger's handwriting in the register; constables apprehended him that same evening at the boardinghouse card table, his winnings still stacked in front of him.
Apprehend is the official word for taking a suspect into custody — more formal than 'catch,' narrower than 'capture,' which can take soldiers, animals, or a chess piece.
Police apprehend a suspect; nobody apprehends a runaway dog.
Apprehend belongs to reports and dispatches; in conversation, officers simply 'catch' or 'arrest' someone.
One caution: apprehend has a second, bookish sense — to grasp with the mind, as in 'she apprehended the danger at once' — so let context show which grip you mean.

On New Year's Day 1845, a suspect fled a Buckinghamshire village and boarded the London train, sure that no rider could outpace a locomotive.
He had not counted on the electric telegraph, newly strung beside the very tracks that were carrying him.
A clerk tapped out his description -- the brown greatcoat, the seat in the last carriage -- and the message reached Paddington station well before the train did.
Officers were waiting on the platform to apprehend him the moment he stepped down, and he was tried within the month.
Newspapers marveled less at the capture than at the means: for the first time, a wire had outrun a fugitive and quietly closed the door ahead of him.
